name: Imipenem/cilastatin
route_note: IV infusion every 6–8 hours; also available combined with relebactam (Recarbrio).

discovery.note: Thienamycin, the parent carbapenem, was isolated from Streptomyces cattleya; imipenem is its stable N-formimidoyl derivative.

tagline: The first carbapenem, paired with cilastatin to stop renal breakdown
summary: Imipenem was the first carbapenem antibiotic, derived from thienamycin discovered at Merck. It is co-administered with cilastatin, which blocks its degradation by renal dehydropeptidase-I, and has very broad activity against Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria.
mechanism: Imipenem binds penicillin-binding proteins, particularly PBP2, causing rapid loss of cell-wall integrity and lysis. It is stable to most serine beta-lactamases apart from carbapenemases.

Cilastatin has no antibacterial activity. It inhibits dehydropeptidase-I in the brush border of the proximal tubule, preventing imipenem hydrolysis, raising urinary concentrations and reducing nephrotoxicity of the metabolites.
uses: Complicated urinary tract, bone, joint and skin infections
Infections due to resistant Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas
Some nontuberculous mycobacterial infections (e.g. Mycobacterium abscessus)

history.title: Thienamycin
history.detail: Merck scientists isolate thienamycin from Streptomyces cattleya; it proves too unstable for use.

history.title: US approval
history.detail: The FDA approves imipenem/cilastatin (Primaxin), the first carbapenem.

history.title: Meropenem
history.detail: Meropenem, a carbapenem stable to DHP-I and not requiring cilastatin, is approved in the US.

history.title: WHO Essential Medicines
history.detail: Imipenem/cilastatin is listed on the WHO EML as a therapeutic alternative to meropenem.

history.title: Imipenem-relebactam
history.detail: The FDA approves imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam (Recarbrio) for complicated urinary and intra-abdominal infections.

pk.metabolism: imipenem hydrolysed by DPEP1 without cilastatin

serious: Seizures, particularly with high doses, CNS disease or renal impairment

facts: Thienamycin was named after the thioether in its structure and its producer, Streptomyces cattleya.
